units: the person the message is addressed to teaches a manual trade to beginners
the beginners lose control of the movement as soon as they are no longer guided
the writer blames the way the trade is taught rather than the learners
the demonstration is at present given in one stretch, with no pause
the proposed remedy is to break the run of movements into three parts
each part ends with a noticeable cue that the learner can check unaided
a short marking sheet, filled in by the learner, tells a clean result from a rough one
the writer advises keeping the breakdown in writing for the next group
text: Dear colleague, I have finally got round to your question about the learners who lose the movement the moment you let go of their hands. The fault sits in the teaching, not in them. You run through the whole sequence in one stretch, then ask them to give it back in a single go, and the memory of the movement cannot carry that much. Break the run into three parts, and end each part with a cue they can notice on their own: the tool coming to rest at a set angle, or a sound the material makes. They stop, they check, they carry on. Add a short marking sheet they fill in themselves, so that a clean result is never taken for a rough one. After a week of fumbling most of them will hold the whole run unaided. Put your breakdown on paper and keep it, because the next group will need it. Tell me how it stands up at your bench.

units: the first question sets teaching one to one against teaching a whole group
one to one bends the pace to the learner and catches a mistake as it appears
the group puts the learner in front of the reasoning of the others
the group forces everyone to say out loud what they thought they had mastered
one to one is expensive because it ties up one trainer for each learner
the group shares the effort but thins out the trainer's attention
the managers questioned advise alternating the two arrangements
one and the same marking scale applied to both arrangements distorts the comparison
text: A listener asks whether teaching one to one beats teaching a whole group. The answer turns on what you choose to measure. Working one to one bends the pace to the learner and catches a mistake as it appears, before it hardens into a habit. A group does something else. It puts each learner in front of the reasoning of the others, and it makes everyone say out loud what they had assumed they knew. A second question turns to cost. One trainer for each learner is a costly arrangement, and that is what keeps it rare, whereas a group shares the effort out but thins the trainer's attention. Must one be chosen? The managers questioned favour alternating the two. The group session lays down the common ground, the private hour clears the blockages it leaves standing. A last question concerns marking. One scale for both distorts the comparison, since they aim at different things.

units: a man working at a bookbinding workshop reports a conversation with a visitor
the visitor wanted to know what the training covered
the man sorts the learning into three groups
the first group covers knowledge of materials and of marks left by old workshops
the second group covers carrying out the movements
the third group rests on stamina, and that is the one that makes people give up
half the apprentices give up before the end of their first season
the departures come when the apprentice is asked to decide with no model to follow
the man judges success by the absence of fingermarks on the leather
text: A man who works at a bookbinding workshop described a conversation he had with a visitor. She wanted to know what the training actually covered. He told her it falls into three sorts of thing. The first is the material: telling one paper from another, picking a glue, reading the marks an old workshop left behind. The second is the hand: folding without crushing, sewing at an even tension, pressing a cover without bruising it. The third, he said, is stamina, and stamina is what sends people away. She asked how many give up. Half of them, he said, go before their first season is out, usually at the point where nobody shows them anything any more and they have to decide for themselves. She asked what best marks out a good one. He pointed at the leather. A steady hand, he said, leaves no fingermarks on it at all.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: at the outset the learner lodged with the master in order to learn a trade
the learner watched for several seasons before being allowed a tool
trade bodies then imposed set stages and a fixed length of training
the learner had to put a piece of work before the judgement of established craftsmen
a refusal obliged the learner to start the piece again
as workshops grew, the master could no longer follow each learner
the methods of the trade were then written down in books
technical schools took over, with syllabuses and examinations
the change brought steadiness and lost some of the attention given to one learner
text: To begin with, learning a trade was nothing like school. You moved in with a master, slept under his roof, and watched him work for whole seasons before anyone let you touch a tool. Then came the trade bodies, which pinned the thing down with set stages and a set length of training. You had to put a piece of work in front of established craftsmen and wait for their verdict, and if they turned it down you started it again. Workshops grew, and no master could keep an eye on every learner any more, so the tricks of the hand went into books and the learner had to puzzle them out alone. Last came the technical schools, with their syllabuses, their classes and their examinations. Every step bought steadiness and gave away a little of the care an old master could spend on one learner. Nobody has settled that argument yet.

units: reading a chapter again gives the false impression of having mastered it
the familiarity of the text is mistaken for having learnt it
rereading draws on recognition whereas the paper calls for recall
because recognition comes easily, the learner stops revising too soon
the learner then finds the gaps at the moment of sitting the paper
saying the content back with the book shut brings the gaps out
the difficulty felt during recall strengthens what is held in memory
the practical consequence is to turn every page into a question put to oneself
learners drilled that way hold more a year later without revising any more
text: Read a chapter over again and it begins to feel like yours. The words come easily, the eye slides on, and that smoothness gets mistaken for something held in memory. Researchers who study learning point to where the muddle starts. Rereading leans on recognition, while the paper calls for recall, and the two are not the same act at all. Recognition costs nothing, so revision stops early and the gaps only show up over the answer sheet. Shut the book, try to say the chapter back, and the opposite happens. It costs something, the holes appear at once, and that very struggle is what fixes the trace. A practical rule follows from it: turn every page you have read into a question you put to yourself. Learners drilled that way still hold more a year on, without having spent an hour more on revision.

units: a learner was stuck on the same line throughout the session
his voice weakened as his discomfort grew
the usual teacher took him for a slow learner
a teacher standing in for a while looked at the way he held the page
the learner tilted the sheet and followed the line with his fingernail
the teacher gave him a strip of card with an opening cut in it
the opening laid over the line stopped the words from running together
the learner first said the letters one by one, then read a whole sentence
the teacher left an account of the method on a card in a drawer
text: The boy had been stuck on the same line since the very start of the session. He ground out the syllables, went back, lost his place, and his voice thinned as the discomfort in it rose. His own teacher had simply written him off as a slow reader. A woman standing in for a week watched the way he held the page. He tilted the sheet and ran a fingernail under the line. She handed him a strip of card with a slot cut in it. He slid the slot along the line, and the words stopped running into one another. He spelled at first, then joined the syllables, then read a whole sentence without stopping for breath. She said nothing about any of it, but she wrote the method on a card and left it in the drawer of the front desk. Two seasons on, the boy was reading aloud to his class without a stumble.

units: the reader must pick one of the two methods and stay with it
the first method rests on writing the list out again and again
once the list is covered, it is written from memory and then checked
the first method suits lists that are short
the second method consists of making cards with a question and an answer
the answer is given aloud and the cards already mastered are set aside
the second method holds off forgetting better on long lists
the same mock test a week later decides between the two methods
using both together would make it impossible to tell which one worked
text: Before you set about learning a list of terms, pick one of the two methods below and stay with it to the end. The first is copying. Write the list out in full, cover it over, then put down again whatever comes back to you. Check it against the original, cross out what went wrong, and start over on a clean sheet. It puts the hand to work, and it serves well when the list is short. The second is questioning. Cut the list into cards, one idea to a card, the question on the front and the answer on the back. Shuffle them, answer aloud, and set aside the ones that give you no trouble. Over a long list this second method holds off forgetting better. Sit the same mock test a week later, and keep whichever leaves you hesitating less. Do not run both at once in that first week, or you will never know which of them did the work.

units: a training centre housed in a former market hall received reporters
its head set out three pieces of work under way
the first concerns taking in adults who are moving to another trade
half of those adults have not studied since they left school
the second rearranged the workshops so that every work station is in view
that visibility makes dangerous handling easier to watch over
the third brings forward the checking of what has been learnt, judged too late
a short check now closes each session and gives the learner a point of comparison
mentoring by former learners is meant to bring down the number who give up
text: A training centre housed in a former market hall has opened its doors to reporters. Its head set out three pieces of work under way. The first is recruitment. The centre now takes in adults moving from one trade to another, half of whom have not studied since the day they left school. The second is the building. Workshops have been rearranged so that every work station can be seen from the central aisle, which makes dangerous handling far easier to watch over. The third is the checking of what has been learnt, which trainers had complained came far too late. A short check now closes each session and gives the learner something to measure against. Asked about learners who give up, she granted that there are still many in the first season, and announced mentoring run by former learners, who know the obstacles from having cleared them.

units: a low room with whitewashed walls serves as a writing workshop for adults
each table is laid out with a sheet, a pencil and a book of models
the tutor draws a letter of unusual size on the board
the participants leaf through the book of models before writing anything
each of them then copies the letter ten times over, watching the tilt of the pencil
halfway through the session, the tutor puts the wrists back in position
the strokes become steadier as the session goes on
each of them cuts out their best line and pastes it into a shared notebook
the shared notebook hangs near the way into the room
text: A low room with whitewashed walls serves as a writing workshop for a group of adults. Before anyone arrives, each table is laid out with a blank sheet, a sharpened pencil and a book of models. The tutor opens the shutters, then draws a letter on the board at an unusual size. The others come in, settle down, and begin by leafing through the book of models without writing a thing. Each of them then copies the letter ten times over, keeping an eye on the tilt of the pencil. Halfway through, the tutor walks between the rows and puts the wrists back in position. The sheets fill with strokes that are ragged at first and steadier later. At the end, everyone cuts out their best line and pastes it into a shared notebook that hangs by the way in. The room empties, the pencils go back in their box, and the notebook keeps the record.

units: the writer disputes the idea of replacing general subjects with short courses
those short courses are cut to fit one particular job
what a job consists of changes over the course of a working life
training fitted too closely becomes useless once the equipment changes
the lasting abilities are getting through a hard manual and reasoning over a drawing
putting a precise question to a colleague is one of those lasting abilities
these abilities come by a long detour and look useless while they are being taught
that apparent uselessness makes them easy to cut from syllabuses
the writer holds that practice with no theoretical detour turns out interchangeable operatives
text: Everyone repeats that school ought to prepare people for work, and a hasty conclusion gets drawn from it. Scrap the general subjects, the argument runs, and put in short courses cut to fit one particular job. The intention is decent enough. The result is ruinous. What a job consists of will not stay the same across a working life, and training tailored that closely is worth nothing the moment the equipment changes. What lasts is the ability to get through a hard manual, to reason over a drawing, to put a clean question to the person at the next bench. Such things are picked up by a long detour, and they look useless at the very moment they are taught, which is what makes them easy to cut. So we save on what prepares people best, and pay later in retraining that fails. A workshop with no detour through theory turns out operatives that anyone could swap for anyone else.
